abstract: >
  Plant biodiversity is under pressure from multiple global change drivers including climate warming, atmospheric nitrogen deposition, and land-use change such as shifting grazing regimes.
  Several of these drivers affect plant biodiversity through the same underlying mechanism, namely impacts on community biomass.
  We hyopothesize that by using community biomass as a common currency we can simplify the direct and indirect effects of multiple global change drivers.
  We test this prediction in a replicated field experiment in alpine and sub-alpine grasslands, simulating the effects of three common global change drivers: climate warming (transplantation to lower elevation), nitrogen deposition (N addition), grazing, and land-use change (simulated grazing by clipping). 
  We found that the three global change drivers affect community biomass and diversity, but the impact depended on the site and the limiting resources.
  The three global change drivers operated indeed on diversity through community biomass, but only at the alpine site where the grassland was both temperature and nutrient limited.
  Using environmental affinities to describe change in envrionmental niches of these communities reveiled that warming and nitrogen addition led to communities with higher competitive ability for nutrients and light.
  At the sub-alpine community, warming led to less shade tolerant and moist communities, while high levels of nitrogen addition led to more acidic soils. 
  Overall, our study showed that global change drivers operate through similar mechanisms when resources are limited.
